On this page

Program 0: Hello CLI ​

This command handler lives in the console profile's command source tree. The binary, main.rs, build script, and profile setup are explained in How a Feluqa CLI Is Structured.

A note on what you are learning: This first program introduces ideas that appear across Rust projects: crate roots, imports, library paths, Result, attributes, functions, references, and return values. Knowing these basics will help you read a wide range of Rust code. Each project may add its own APIs and concepts, so use this as a foundation rather than a complete guide to every part of Rust.

Command handler ​

The CLI application scaffold is planned but is not available yet. Once it supports console applications, create this file from the project root:

text
src/commands/hello.rs

Paste the following handler into that file:

This handler is named hello; with the hello-cli binary, the user runs hello-cli hello:

rust
// Disable Rust's implicit standard, extern-crate, macro_use, and tool preludes.
// Names used below are imported or qualified explicitly.
#![no_implicit_prelude]
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]   // Forbid unsafe Rust code throughout this crate.
#![deny(unused_must_use)] // Treat ignored results marked #[must_use] as compilation errors.
#![deny(missing_docs)]    // Require documentation for public items.

extern crate core;              // Make the core crate available explicitly.
extern crate feluqa;            // Make the Feluqa crate available explicitly.
use ::core::result::Result::Ok; // Import the Ok variant from Rust's core library.
use feluqa::console::{
    echo,
    CommandContext,
    CommandResult,
    OutputStyle,
};

/// Prints the first greeting from this console application.
#[feluqa::command(
    name = "hello",
    description = "Print a greeting",
    context = "anywhere",
)]
fn hello(
    // Mutable reference to the command's execution context.
    // The leading underscore indicates that it is intentionally unused.
    _context: &mut CommandContext<'_>,
) -> CommandResult {
    // Write a plain-text message to the Feluqa console.
    echo(
        "Hello CLI",
        OutputStyle::Plain,
    );

    // Return success without an associated value.
    // Ok = success; () = unit value (no meaningful data).
    // An error would instead be returned with Err(error).
    Ok(())
}

Rust's core, alloc, and std libraries ​

Rust's libraries form layers. core provides fundamental types and traits without requiring an operating system or heap allocation. alloc adds heap-backed types and requires an allocator. std builds on these libraries with operating-system facilities such as files, networking, threads, and I/O.

text
std   operating-system services and higher-level APIs
└── alloc   heap-backed types such as String, Vec, and Box
    └── core   fundamental types and traits such as Result, Option, and Iterator
LibraryProvidesExamples
coreFundamental types, traits, and operations; no OS or heap requirement.Result, Option, Iterator
allocHeap allocation abstractions and heap-backed collections; needs an allocator, not necessarily an OS.String, Vec, Box
stdThe standard library's OS integration and higher-level facilities.File, TcpStream, thread

std re-exports many items from core, so core::result::Result and std::result::Result name the same type. Feluqa code can use core when it wants a fundamental Rust type without making that type's path depend on std.

Explicit crate paths and the prelude ​

A Rust prelude is a set of names made available without a use statement. Rust has several preludes; the standard prelude is why ordinary Rust code can often write Option or Result without an import. Feluqa uses #![no_implicit_prelude] to suppress implicit prelude imports, so this example explicitly brings the core crate into scope and imports Ok from it.

The leading :: in ::core::result::Result::Ok starts resolution from the external crate namespace in Rust 2018 and later. It makes clear that core means Rust's external crate, even if the application also has a local module named core. The leading :: affects name resolution; it does not select a different library. It is useful for this explicit path, but is not required on every import.

rust
extern crate core;
use ::core::result::Result::{Ok, Err};

fn example() -> ::core::result::Result<(), &'static str> {
    Ok(())
}

In the command above, extern crate core; makes the crate available despite the disabled extern prelude, and use ::core::result::Result::Ok; makes the success variant available as Ok(()). The same convention can be used for Feluqa APIs: import the items a command needs, while keeping their crate origin visible.

The example uses the current CommandContext, CommandResult, and echo contracts. The console dispatches to the handler, which writes Hello CLI and returns a result. The command's namespace and arguments are parsed before the handler runs; later commands can call services, inspect options, or perform longer operations without changing how the binary starts.

Why these crate attributes ​

These crate-level rules are the recommended starting point for Feluqa Rust code:

AttributeWhy use it
#![no_implicit_prelude]Disables Rust's implicit prelude imports. Import or qualify the names the crate uses so dependencies stay visible and generated code is predictable.
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]Prevents unsafe blocks in application code, keeping memory-safety boundaries small and visible.
#![deny(unused_must_use)]Rejects silently ignored results from operations that may fail or require action. Handle the result or explicitly explain why it can be discarded.
#![deny(missing_docs)]Requires documentation on public APIs so generated help and reference docs explain what the API does and why it exists.

Run Program 0 ​

From the project root, run the binary with the hello command:

sh
cargo run -- hello

The console prints:

text
Hello CLI

Congratulations! You have created and run your first Feluqa console command. The hello handler is registered with the hello-cli binary and uses Feluqa's console API to write its output.
